summary: Defines common semantics and data formats for instant messaging to make it easier to build gateways between services. Many instant messaging protocols existed, and this profile gives a shared model for sending messages between them.

plainLanguage.summary: Different chat apps used different languages. This document makes a shared message language so a translator can connect them.

questions: what is the im uri scheme
subtitle: A shared abstract model for instant messages so gateways can connect different messaging services.

tldr.problem: Many instant messaging protocols were in use and little interoperability between their services had been achieved.
tldr.mechanism: CPIM defines abstract message and response operations, im: addresses, a hop counter against loops and a common end-to-end message format, so gateways can relay content between services.
tldr.outcome: A protocol that supports each operation can interface with CPIM gateways, and secure messages can keep end-to-end protection through them using S/MIME.

today: RFC 3860 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Common Profile for Gateways
sections.content:
At the time of writing, numerous instant messaging protocols were in use and little interoperability between them had been achieved. The Common Profile for Instant Messaging (CPIM) defines semantics and data formats for common instant messaging services, to make gateways between services easier to build. Instant messaging itself is defined in RFC 2778.

Behavior is described abstractly, as operations between the consumer and provider of a service. Each IM service must say how those operations map onto its own protocol. How it does so is a local matter, provided there is a clear relation to the abstract behavior. The abstract attributes also need a concrete encoding in each service, which could be textual key/value pairs, a compact binary form or nested containers.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not invent a new chat app. It describes the basic moves every chat app already makes, so a go-between can connect them.

sections.title: Gateways and What a Compliant Protocol Must Offer
sections.content:
A CPIM gateway is a network element that interworks between diverse instant messaging protocols. Under this model the protocols carry a common payload that the gateway relays. A client may not know whether the service it addresses is an endpoint or an intermediary gateway, because responses from either look the same.

To interface with a gateway, an IM protocol must support all the operations in the memo, meaning it has some message or capability that provides each one. The attributes must correspond to information the protocol has. These attributes are the minimum needed for interoperability, and the protocol's own functions may carry extra information that CPIM does not map.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is a translator standing between two chat apps. Each app must be able to do the same few basic things for the translator to work.

sections.title: The Message and Response Operations
sections.content:
To send to an INSTANT INBOX, an application invokes the message operation. Its attributes are source, destination, MaxForwards and TransID, plus the message content. The TransID correlates a message with its response, and gateways should handle TransIDs up to 40 bytes long. The memo assumes the underlying protocols deliver messages reliably and adds no delivery assurance of its own.

The service immediately answers with a response operation carrying the same TransID and a status. It first checks that source and destination are syntactically valid INSTANT INBOXes, that the destination can be resolved (unless it is the final recipient), and that access control permits the request. Any failed check gives status failure.

If the checks pass, the status is success if the message was delivered and failure if it could not be. If delivery was delegated, as with a gateway or proxy, and no authoritative indication will come back, the status is indeterminant. If an indication will come back, the response is sent once it arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand a note to the post office and they immediately tell you if it worked, failed, or if they passed it along and cannot say yet. A ticket number ties the answer to your note.

sections.title: IM Addresses and the im: Scheme
sections.content:
An INSTANT INBOX is named with an im: URI, for example im:fred@example.com. A client finds the next hop by resolving the domain name part of the destination, and implementations SHOULD follow the URI dereferencing guidelines in RFC 3861.

The syntax follows the mailto: URI: IM-URI = "im:" [ to ] [ headers ], where to is a mailbox as defined in RFC 2822. Using an IM URI is meant to start the user's messaging application with the destination and headers filled in. IANA assigned the im scheme.

For gateway design, the memo's appendix says mappings that put special information into the local part MUST use the meta-syntax of RFC 2846. A simple technique is source routing, which puts the whole original address in the local part and names the gateway in the domain part, such as im:pepp=example.com/fred@relay-domain. It has a history of operational problems, and the memo advises hiding the mapping from end users.
sections.plainLanguage: An im: address is like an email address for a chat mailbox. To reach a mailbox in another network, the address can be wrapped inside the translator's address.

sections.title: Content and the Common Message Format
sections.content:
CPIM defines semantics rather than syntax, but some properties, especially security, need a common end-to-end format. So applications sending message operations to a CPIM gateway MUST implement the format in MSGFMT (RFC 3862), and MAY support others.

CPIM gateways MUST be able to relay message content between supported protocols without modifying or inspecting it.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone puts the note in the same kind of envelope, the translator can pass it along sealed without reading it.

sections.title: Preventing Message Loops
sections.content:
Dynamic routing can send a message through a relay more than once. Loops are hard to detect, since aliases and group list expansion can legitimately do this. The memo assumes gateway-able protocols have something equivalent to an integer for the maximum number of hops.

A gateway decrements MaxForwards each time it relays a message. No initial value is mandated, but it is recommended to be reasonably large (over one hundred). If a gateway receives a message with MaxForwards of 0, it discards it and invokes a failure operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each translator crosses off one number from the note. When it reaches zero, the note is thrown away so it cannot go in circles forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security for instant messaging is covered in RFC 2779. CPIM gateways MUST meet the minimum security requirements of the protocols they connect. Gateways add new risks. End-to-end confidentiality and integrity can only be kept through a gateway if the protocols share a common message format such as MSGFMT.

When end-to-end security is required, the message operation MUST use MSGFMT and MUST protect the MSGFMT MIME body with S/MIME, using encryption and/or signatures. AES should be preferred, but only the baseline algorithms mandated by S/MIME and CMS are required. Certificates for S/MIME IM use SHOULD carry the subject's IM URI in a subjectAltName field, and widely accepted trust anchors are encouraged. Anonymous messaging is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: To keep a note private all the way through the translator, lock it in a secret envelope that only the receiver can open.
